utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, do you claim that there was no shelter available for civilians and that wherever individuals were found to reside outside of their own residences, were, in fact, places of detention?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were basements in the various houses that could be deemed shelters. Now, as for their safety, that's a different issue. The locations I cited were places where captured civilians were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statements, you say that I said that should there be a war, only one people would stay behind. Are you referring here to my address to the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina on 15 October 1991?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You said on that occasion that should there be a war, that you were afraid or rather you said that the Muslims would not be able to defend themselves. By saying so, you sent a message across to the effect that you knew that the Muslims did not have weapons, whereas you were certain that the Serbs did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were referring there to this speech of mine and no other?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you did add, if I can be allowed to say so, that in that event, Bosnia would disappear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So would you say that I was war-mongering there or was I in fact speaking against the war with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you did send a message across to the Muslims. This was during an attempt in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina to reach an agreement about the referendum. So this was shortly before the referendum that you disagreed with. And when I say you, I mean the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this your interpretation of the speech, or did you merely adopt a position on my speech that had been taken up by the Muslim leadership or the SDA?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic, all the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Yugoslavia carried this speech of yours. It was a very strong message you sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your understanding was that I was, in fact, encouraging Muslims to wage a war with us?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the context was, but it is -- it can be easily concluded your meaning, that is, when you said that one people would disappear in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I was dissuading them from the war option and not persuading them to opt for it. And did you not notice that Muhamed Filipovic said what you just said I said at an earlier session when he said that should a war broke out my people would disappear?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember what Mr. Filipovic said but I do remember clearly what you said. You were aware of the fact that the Serb people had received weapons from the JNA and that it was very nearly ready for a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did I say that should a war break out the Muslims would not be able to defend themselves because they will have the Serbs and the Croats on the other side and did they not in fact enter into a conflict with both these sides?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put several questions to me there. Let me answer your first question. You said, always, in all the rallies to the Serbs that they know how to fight and that they will know how to defend the Serb land and Bosnia-Herzegovina was the Serb land and their enemies were Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats. So in this context, the idea was that the war would be waged against the Muslims and the Croats, because they were in favour of a different option, that is, the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, we have all my speeches here and there is no need for either you or me to qualify them. What I'm asking you is this: Did I not ask in this speech of mine that we should not decide for the war option and that the Muslims would not be able to defend themselves from the two fires, i.e. the Serbs and the Croats? Is this not something that I said?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already commented on this, and I believe that I was clear. You are setting out theses of sorts. You know that by that point there was a war on between Yugoslavia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did not the Muslims at a later stage wage a war against the Serbs and the Croats and Abdic's Muslims and that they got less than what had been on offer with the Lisbon agreement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, when Tudjman and Milosevic drew up a plan to divide Bosnia-Herzegovina, a conflict broke out between the Croats and Bosnian Muslims in a part of Herzegovina and Central Bosnia, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you do know for a fact that Tudjman and Milosevic were the ones who agreed on it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a fact. First in Karadjordje and later in Klagenfurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this is a fact that you accept but you'd heard it from the media or do you have any other source?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it from the media, and it was mentioned repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it not true that you were registered by the Red Cross while you were detained?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was hidden away with a group of 12 prisoners in the KP Dom Foca. In the morning hours of the 23rd of June, 1993, we were taken to the basement of a bakery that was located right by the KP Dom. We were not registered by the ICRC. However, the prisoners who were registered were the ones who were throughout that time members of a work platoon who were forced to do farm work. However, there was a group that was hidden away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, finally, you were registered, you were registered when you were in Kula as well, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we arrived in Kula, after a while, I was registered. Not immediately, though, because we had to wait for some reason. Seven or 10 days went by and then the International Red Cross arrived and then I was registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you testified in another case, this is not disclosing your identity because many people testified in the trial of president Milosevic, you said that many paramilitary formations took part in what happened in Foca, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I've said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what their names were and how they were marked in some way?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were called the Guard. I think they were from Uzice. Then there were Seselj's men and Arkan's men. However, as far as insignia are concerned, I said in my previous statement that I could never remember these insignia of theirs and their ranks and whatever. To tell you the truth, I was never interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that a certain Muslim named Salko was beaten by mistake?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An attempt was made to slit his throat in a room that was assigned for prison torture. Somebody else saw that this was not that Salko Mandzo because there had been this other Salko Mandzo and this man was released. He came to my room and he had this cut on his throat. Not very deep but nevertheless there was this cut.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who saved him, who indicated that it was the wrong man?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the guards present there or one of the military policemen who were torturing people in this room. This was psychological and physical torture against the detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find out what this Salko Mandzo was guilty of? Was this some kind of revenge for something that had happened before?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man who survived and who was brought to my room after that attempt to have him slaughtered, he explained all the things that happened to him, whereas this other Salko Mandzo, I didn't even know him so I don't know whether they had a particular intention in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At any rate, there was some difference between these two Salko Mandzos. One they thought was guilty and the other one they thought was not guilty and when they realised that this was the one who was not guilty they let him go.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement, this statement of yours, 4226, on page 8, you said that you had been registered by the Red Cross, and then you say that after that register you were discovered by the Red Cross, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You got the two confused. Let me explain. Considerably before the Red Cross came, and before we found out about this, we actually did not know that the Red Cross would come on 23 June. Let me point this out. Take a look at the date when we were detained, 11 April 1992. It was only on 23 June 1993 that the International Red Cross was allowed to come and visit the camps in Foca. That is where we can see this obstruction and this ban placed on the International Red Cross and other humanitarian organisations that wanted to visit prisoners. As for this list that you are referring to, it was compiled in a smart way, if I can put it that way. They went from room to room so that prisoners would say what their ailments were. The explanation provided was that they would be exchanged. People believed that. And the male nurse was writing down names and he was saying what kind of ailments people had. However, these people were not exchanged then. On the contrary, they stayed on, though they were ill and were exchanged only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to deal with that another time with other witnesses. Tell me, do you know that I issued an order already in June to all local civilian and police authorities stating that they have to give access to the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know about that, but do show us that order of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D4207. Could we have that, please? The original has already been admitted, and this is a telegram that was sent on the basis of that order. 4207. Now, do you know that from the month of April 1992, until April 1993, about 1,100 Serbs lost their lives in Foca?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We can question that particular figure. I said that they established work platoons consisting of unskilled, skilled and highly skilled workers, immediately after the arrest. And they were taken out for forced labour every day. This was a rather large group, consisting of 50 or 60 of them. One of these groups included the people who went to the textile factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I haven't finished yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The question was whether 1.100 Serbs lost their lives in Foca and I think you answered the question. Your next question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please take a look at this document which is actually a telegram, a telegraphic transformation of the original that we have already admitted. Could you please take a look at the Serbian version? It says there that delegates of the International Red Cross should have safe passage and that all of those who do not abide by this will be punished.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see the date. When did you issue this? On the screen, I cannot see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the date is June and that was in the media, too. However, the date was not placed here intentionally so that people would not think that it was dated or obsolete.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let us proceed under the assumption that you actually did send this telegram. However, this never actually started working in practice on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With regard to your previous answer, you said that you know that there was this figure of 1,100 Serbs that was bandied about but you say that that's debatable. So what do you think, how many Serbs got killed in Foca during that one year?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can certainly not present my opinion. I was in camp for so long that I cannot even make an assumption as to how many Serbs could have lost their lives. The lady I know who introduced herself as the director at the time to the work platoon, she mentioned that figure in the context of Serbs getting killed, not only Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what happened with Serbs and their leadership in the neighbouring municipality of Gorazde before your arrest?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know nothing in particular. I know that there was a conflict there too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Time is limited, Mr. Karadzic. Come to your relevant questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give the number of the original order you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are looking for it, this is a telegraphic version of that order. I think it has already been admitted. This public call and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking for the number for the record. I take it there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but I just want to take note there is no date, there is definitely not a date June in there and I do not recall any corresponding order but there may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking for the Exhibit number we admitted. Yes, we will admit this and in the meantime I would like you to inform us the exhibit number. We will give the number for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D1692.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know how the Serb village of Josanica near Foca fared? Do you know that the Serbs there were killed, that the village was set on fire, and do you know that all the Serb civilians that the Muslim army came across were killed, and no prisoners were taken?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From April 1992 until -- until there weren't any Serbs left.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Serbs were in Foca always, and in the territory of the municipality of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in Josanica they were killed and that their houses were burned?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know that tens of persons from the Serb family of Elez were killed as soon as the war started?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Where did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you know that the Elezes live in Miljevina and around Miljevina. They were killed in their own houses, in their own villages, tens of Elezes were killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The Elezes lived around Miljevina but there were less of them. There weren't tens of them there and I'm not aware of them falling victim that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what I'm going to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Put your case. I will allow you to put your case but I was about to question the relevance of this question, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On 23 June Dragan Elez was killed, 24 years old; Novo Elez, 13 years old; Milorad Elez, 59 years old; Ilija Kovac, 46 years old; Milanko Ljubovic, 29 years old; Njegos Savic, 21, from the village of Jamici; and then Dragan Solaja, 19 from Modro Polje; then Milovan Elez was wounded; and the wounded Njegos Savic was ultimately killed by an ax.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have to intervene again. How is this relevant to your case, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I stand accused of things that happened in their area and that had been happening for centuries. I have been accused, and the picture that was portrayed was that the savage Serbs attacked the tame Muslims for no reason whatsoever. They have been exterminating each other for five centuries. What happened in the Second World War happened in this war too and I want to see here and now who ordered this. Did events simply stem from one another or did this have something to do with the authorities of Republika Srpska? In my view, this is highly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, reading out the names and ages of people who were killed, however sad that is, seems to me to take us absolutely nowhere. If what you are really doing is seeking to find out who ordered it, i.e. who may be responsible as a matter of law, that's another topic but I haven't heard anything that goes to that issue yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this witness is certainly going to deny everything that the Muslims did. But I wish to remind him of what had happened. Does he know about this or is he denying it? That's what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know -- actually you mentioned that some people were on a killing spree, whereas Krnojelac and these commanders were saving people from them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. I did not put it that way, in that context, that somebody came to save someone. Guards or policemen came in to the rooms, those who were on regular duty, and they took some people out and then these people simply went missing. Of course, I haven't seen some people, for example, Mr. Krnojelac. I did not see him trying to stop this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say -- actually, Mr. Witness, there is this pattern on the basis of which it says this man was taken out and he never reappeared or there has been no trace of him. Are you trying to say that they were not released, are you trying to say that they were killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exhumations and other analyses proved that later that that is exactly what happened to the people who were taken out and who then went missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is another pattern as well in the statements of all of you. Somebody is taken out and then a gunshot was heard. Nobody saw a murder, a gunshot was heard and your conclusion is that somebody was killed.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that happened in front of the building and we could not see it from our rooms. De facto we could not see this through the thick walls that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far away is the prison from the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my estimate would be, say, 50 or 80 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How steep are the banks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Opposite the KP Dom, they weren't very steep, and sometimes during the rain, when it would rain, the Drina could even flood the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you say in your statements that something would fall into the Drina and on the basis of that noise, you would conclude that a man had been thrown into the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that was from the bridge. There was a metal bridge called the iron bridge, in the immediate vicinity of the KP Dom. Of course, that is much higher up. And of course that is what we heard. People who were in the rooms above my room. And we were all closely following what happened after persons were taken out. From 13 June until 30 June 1992, when people were being taken out, that usually happened during the night. It was a rather large group of 30 to 35 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to my question. So you hear a thump or you hear a sound and your conclusion is that a man was thrown into the river.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But if later on people find that person in Gorazde or Visegrad or further down or last year in the lake of Perucac that is confirmation of that having happened. Also, my relative called Jusuf, who we discussed yesterday, that is how his death was established too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On 19 and 20 December, were many dead and wounded Serb civilians from the area of Josanica brought to the Foca hospital? Josanica is about 20 kilometres away from Foca, about 63 corpses of civilians, women, children, everyone?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about that. Never heard of it. Just tell me what the period is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: December 1992.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You heard shots around Foca. You spoke about that. You heard shots on the hill slopes around Foca. Do you know who Alija Siljak is?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alija Siljak is a person who was known to the authorities, and I did not see him in Foca before the war or over the past five or ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that he was the vice-president of the Ustasha Croatian Party of Rights and he doesn't hide that fact and that he was a member of the had HOS which was an armed formation and that HOS was present in Foca, that it had its camps there for Muslims on the hill slopes?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know and I didn't know that he was a member of the HOS. I was not aware of the existence of such camps on the hill slopes around Foca. The fact is, however, that in Croatia this organisation did exist. There was, indeed, HOS in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your time is up, the three hours we allotted originally and I can sense you're coming to an end. How much do you need to conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Some ten minutes or so, not longer than that, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As a high official in Foca you're saying that you don't know that there were 2.000 well-armed combatants in Foca and its surroundings and that they had been trained by people who were members of the HOS under the leadership of Alija Siljak. You're saying that you don't know that there were training camps around Foca and in Tijetista [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if there had been such a strong formation of HOS, I'm sure that Foca would not have fallen that fast and the whole territory for that matter. At the beginning of our discussion today, we said that Foca was -- is the biggest municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in terms of its size. The president of the Crisis Staff said that the entire territory of the municipality of Foca was conquered on 25 April 1992. And then they said, okay, now we are moving on to Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's then conclude something about the overall negotiations. You were very adamant when you voiced your opinions about some general developments like my speech at the assembly. Were you familiar with my negotiations with Izetbegovic and Zulfikarpasic when we discussed the historical Muslim-Serb agreement? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When was that? Can you give me the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was in July and August 1991. It is a well-published agreement which was nearly signed, but then Izetbegovic withdrew.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The parties were being established at the time. You know when the SDS was established. You know when the SDA was established. I don't know anything about this disagreement of yours. I never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in Foca there were 200.000 Muslims from Bosnia, Sandzak, and Kosovo, and that these people sported a very pronounced Islamic iconography, there was a rally of some 200.000 people at the river mouth?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a rally, but I never read in the media that there were 200.000 people, rather I read about 100.000 people, but I was personally surprised when all these people arrived. As far as I know, there were no appeals launched for people to gather at that rally. Rather, the media had published that the rally would take place, just like they published and announced SDS, SDA and other parties' rallies, they would provide information as to when such rallies would take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a while ago you told us something about the establishment of the parties. I'm talking about 1991, when we already had our joint authorities. Not communist authorities but democratic authorities. Were you familiar with the negotiations which ended in 1992? Do you know how Foca would have looked like according to the Lisbon agreement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, witness. In that case, your general statements about developments are probably based on what you learned from the media. You were not informed about those things by Izetbegovic, you only read about them in the media?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I told you yesterday what my primary task had always been and that was to read the newspapers and I couldn't read all the newspapers. It sufficed for me to listen to the main news in the evening, and the news that I heard in the evening would always be confirmed on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You told us that detainees in Kula were killed. At the hands of who did they die, from whose fire? Was it sniper fire, machine-gun fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The detainees were taken from Kula for forcible labour, and -- and then they would be seriously wounded and they would die of their wounds or they would die of illness, like, for example, a young man who suffered from stress-related diabetes and died.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I am asking you about shelling fire that killed the prisoners. Who opened that fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please, let me tell you who would -- who would fire at us, at Kula, on the first floor there were Serbs and on the ground floor there were us, Muslims. What kind of fire are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did shells fall within the perimeter of Kula?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I, myself, witnessed the fall of one shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the detainees volunteered to go to work, that they liked to go to work because they received more food, they received cigarettes and even drinks?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not excluding that individuals did that. Some people were simply bored. They didn't have anything to do. People were hungry, and they did not -- they suffered greatly from hunger and, yes, they did go to work to receive more food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions. And the document, the original, the instructions or guidelines for the Red Cross, which is D477, please. It was published in the media and you can tell what the date was from the media reports. We will obtain those excerpts as well. And also some witnesses confirmed that, that that was in early 1992, at the beginning of the war, Mandic and some other confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, only on one topic but I would want to put three documents in this context.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday evening Mr. Karadzic asked you about the Foca Tactical Group and he asked you, and this is on page 104, lines 21 to 25, "What army was it part of?" And your answer was that the Serbs had an army and following this question was a discussion about when the Army of Republika Srpska came into being, and you put it and said the TO transformed before -- transformed to become the Army of Republika Srpska. Can we please have 65 ter 07278 on the screen? And is it -- as it is coming up, it is an order of the Foca Tactical Group of 7 July 1992, to break through the siege of Gorazde and if you look at paragraph 2, it refers here to the task with a brigade reinforce the artillery of Foca Tactical Group, shall attack the general Ustikolina-Gorazde direction and so on and so forth and can we have the last page, please? The previous one, please, the previous in the English, the B/C/S is correct. And if you look at the stamp here, what does it say? Can you read it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably we need to zoom in further.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We do have a translation anyway of the stamp. It says the stamp says TO of the Serbian Autonomous District of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of this TO of the Serbian Autonomous District of Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We already said that the Territorial Defence -- or actually the Serbian territorial units became the Army of Republika Srpska in May 1992. I really don't know what is this Territorial Defence of Herzegovina. I don't know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask Madam Prosecutor whether it says here the Serbian Municipality of Foca? The same stamp features those words as well and they have not been translated. Could she perhaps ask the witness to read the outermost circle of the stamp? Does it say here the Serbian Municipality of Foca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't see the word Foca anywhere in this stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be zoomed in even further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We collapse the English page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look at 6.00. Does it say Serbian Municipality of Foca here? Why has this not been translated?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think that's not a question for the witness to answer. I can only say that I can only look at the English version and why only part of the stamp is translated, I think that's a mistake, but it's now clarified and I would like to have this document admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we need -- have we confirmation from the witness that it says Serbian Municipality of Foca? Can you confirm that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. I don't see that. It's not written here anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody who can see can see it written at the bottom between 5 and 7 o'clock, the outer most circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can be clarified with our translation unit. Yes, this will be -- this can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And can we please have 65 ter 23459 on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we give the number for the previous one?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P3354.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There should be a translation as well, at least I have a translation. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as we see it here, it is a combat report of the Foca Tactical Group to the Herzegovina Corps Command and the Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 21 July 1992, and Commander Kovac, again, here is signing for this combat report. He is now reporting, as we can see, to the Herzegovina corps and the VRS Main Staff. Any comments from you, witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The area that is described here is where fighting did take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can this be admitted, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3355, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And one last document and it's also, again, Foca Tactical Group, 65 ter 23460. And this is another combat report dated 31 July 1992, and here we have the Herzegovina Corps reporting to the VRS Main Staff and it refers in paragraph 1 to military operations in the zones of the tactical group Foca and tactical group Kalinovik and it refers here to Trnovo area and Jabuka. And if we look at paragraph 2, it refers to tactical group Foca suffering ten casualties.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: My question to you is: Were you in the prison aware when the Serb soldiers in Foca suffered casualties?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-239 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We felt that because detainees would be taken out, and they would disappear after that. And the second thing that we noticed was that they tried to reduce the usual quantities of food that we received during those periods, but as I said, that reflected mostly on people being taken out in smaller or larger groups. Dr. Cedo Dragovic on one occasion told me that we are in grave danger, and I asked him why? And he said if a Serb should get killed, depending on their military -- on his military rank, three to five Muslims would disappear in turn. And that's what really happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3356, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, this concludes the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, sir, it concludes your evidence. On behalf of this Chamber and the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for your coming to the Tribunal yet again to give it. Now you are free to go. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will rise all together. We will take a break for an hour and resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to inform you that you will be testifying here today with the benefit of pseudonym, which is KDZ-075, as well as image and voice distortion. This means that there will be no reference to your real name or information which might reveal your identity to the public or media. And also, the audiovisual record of your testimony, which is broadcast to the public, will have a distorted image like this, which you will see in front of your monitor, like this. So we -- and your voice will be distorted as well to ensure that your identity is protected and the transcript, while available to the public, will always refer to your pseudonym. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to come closer to the microphone, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 90278 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir there is going to be a document on the screen in front of you. If you look at the sheet you'll see your name, your date of birth, and your pseudonym number in this case. Could you please confirm that that is your name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Yes, the name is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the date of birth?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that for admission under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3357, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, as we discussed, part of your evidence in this case will be submitted in writing and we first need to deal with the formalities related to that submission. You testified as a protected witness in the Krajisnik trial; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You've subsequently had an opportunity to review the audio recordings of your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you were asked today about the matters that you testified to in the Krajisnik trial, would you provide the same information to the Trial Chamber, bearing in mind that even if you couldn't formulate it in exactly the same words, the essence of it would be the same?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Yes. The -- it's more or less the same, yes. Yes, it would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 65 ter number 22697A which is the witness's Krajisnik testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I also tender 65 ter number 22697B which is a public redacted transcript of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Both will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibits P3358 under seal and Exhibit P3359 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honour's leave, I will now read a summary of the witness's evidence. Witness KDZ-075 was born and raised in the Kljuc municipality. He testified about the check-point set up in the areas around his village in March 1992 and the restriction of movement of the population. The witness testified about the arming of the Serb population in 1991 to early 1992 and testified about the dismissal of the Muslim police on 25 May 1992. The witness testified that at the end of May 1992, the Muslim villagers were told to hand in their weapons. Bosko Maric from the SDS in Sanica and a local SDA representative were with the police when they drove around the town making the announcement on a megaphone. The villagers were told that the village would be shelled and someone would be killed if the weapons were not handed in. All of the weapons were then handed over. After the surrender of weapons soldiers came to the village and instructed the witness and other Muslim villagers in the area to put white sheets outside their houses as a sign of loyalty. A number of men were then made to walk in front of two APCs from village to village and had to tell the inhabitants to hang white sheets outside their houses and the houses were then subsequently searched for weapons. The witness testified about the killing of at least 144 people in. Biljani in July 1992 and that is schedule A.7.3. At around 6 a.m. on 10 July the witness awoke to find his village was surrounded by local Serb soldiers. All the men aged between 18 and 60 were ordered to gather in a nearby field. Captain Marko Samardzija and Mladjo Tesic were there with the soldiers. The men were then taken two by two in a column to the primary school in Biljani. As they approached the school the witness could see a large number of Serb soldiers at the school. When they arrived there, the witness saw about ten special policemen. The witness saw the commander of the police station, Mile Tomic there. The Muslim men were searched and were then ordered into one of the classrooms. Around 50 to 70 men were placed in one classroom and their names were written down on a list. After 10 to 15 minutes, ten men were called out individually and after a few minutes, the witness heard bursts of fire. Then the remainder of the men were made to leave the classroom in groups of five. When they groups of five men were taken out, the shelling -- or the shooting intensified. After 20 to 30 men had left the room, panic arose in the classroom because the men feared they were all going to be killed. The witness was taken outside with four other men. They had to pass through a gauntlet of special policemen who were lined up from the school to the bus. He was kicked in the stomach and punched by a person he knew, Dragan Cvijic and hit with batons, sticks, and chains by the other policemen. When the bus was full of people sitting on the seats and on the floor, the witness heard one man say to another, What shall we do with the rest? And one of the chief men sitting near a tree said, We don't need the rest of them, kill them all. One bus is enough. The bus started in the direction of Kljuc but stopped after about ten metres. Four men were taken off the bus. The bus started again but stopped again 50 metres on. They were told that they were being moved on to another bus. Three or four special-purpose military policemen wearing camouflage uniform with white belts came on the bus and ordered the witness and four other men to get off. The five men were then taken a few metres away near a house. As they were being taken toward the house, the witness saw the dead bodies of the four men who had been taken from the bus earlier. Realising that they would be killed, the witness and other men tried to run. The policemen opened fire. The witness fell to the ground and feigned death. Bullets hit the ground around him. He heard the military policemen off those who lay dying around him. The witness stayed still. The bus full of men and those guarding it then left. The witness then heard bursts of fire throughout the whole village. He remained lying there quite still. Around 10 minutes later the witness herd soldiers all around him. There was a cafe in the house and there were people in front of the cafe. Soldiers came back to the house where the witness was lying still. After a while, the soldiers left. For the next two months the witness hid in his village and surrounds before going to the town of Kljuc where he got on a convoy to Travnik, in September 1992. That completes the summary of the witness's written evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, I have a limited number of questions now to expand upon some matters in relation to your written evidence which is now before the Court. At transcript page 4955 to 4956, you testified that check-points were set up in the areas surrounding your village in March 1992. Who set up these check-points?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. In 1992, check-points were set up and the then police or rather or the reserve police force was headed by Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Which ethnicity of people set the check-points up? You just referred to Mile Tomic. What ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Mile Tomic was a Serb. There were also several Muslims at first. Later on, before the month of May, those Muslims were fired, they had to go home, and the check-points were manned by Serbs only from then on. The entire police station was in the hands of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At transcript page 4957, you testified that in April or May you saw military helicopters landing in Serb villages. What if anything did you hear about JNA arming the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: I personally saw when helicopters landed in the hamlet of Gologlav on two occasions. As for the arming of the Serbs I heard that from people or the locals of Sanica, who lived in mixed marriages and they personally bragged that the Serb civilians had been distributed weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the weapons were distributed by the JNA? Do I understand you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Well, they did not say who distributed those weapons, but it is understood that if the helicopter landed in Glogova and Sanica on two occasions that it was either a JNA helicopter or a helicopter that belonged to the then police. I'm not sure actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want you to now look at a document, if 65 ter number 00912 could be brought on the screen, please. Sir, this was a document that you were shown the other day. Are you familiar with the names, the persons named in this document?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: In 80 per cent of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to the people, the 38 people, that are listed on this document? At least of the ones, the 80 per cent that you know?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: I know that they ended up in Manjaca camp and then they were released sometime in late 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were they before they were in the Manjaca camp, do you know?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Before that, they were at home. That was in late May and early June, and as the troops were passing by when we returned, some of those locals were brought to the school. From there to the elementary school in Kljuc. And then according to their own words, they ended up in Manjaca. And then a few months later most of them ended up in the Republic of Croatia, namely in Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3360, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, I now wish to turn to the events which occurred on 10 July 1992. This is detailed in your testimony at transcript pages 4965 to 4984 and I'm not going to ask you to recount that day again. I simply have a few clarifying questions that I wish to ask. At transcript page 4967 to 4968, you testified that when you arrived at the primary school in Biljani you saw hundreds of soldiers around the school and you testified that you saw Mile Tomic the commander of the Sanica police station, his deputy Mihic and around ten special policemen and the director of a factory whose name you couldn't remember. Do you recall deputy Mihic's first name?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: To be honest, before that, he was the owner of a TV repair shop, and we all called him Perica. He had this TV repair shop and he personally came to my house on several occasions to repair my TV. At first he was a civilian, and then he became the police commander deputy, Tomic's deputy. I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The ten or so special policemen that you saw when you arrived at the school, were they part of the military or the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: They were military policemen. They had white belts. And they did not hail from Sanica. They were from Kljuc which means that I didn't really know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At transcript page 4972, you testified that after everyone was put in the school, Mihic started making a list of the names of the men in the classroom. Did he finish making the list?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: No, he did not finish making the list. He was replaced by another policeman, another policeman called Lazic or Laza, continued compiling the list and finally finished the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What position did Lazo hold, do you know?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. He was a member of the reserve police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 11824 on the screen, please? That's not the right document, I'm sorry. I won't be a moment, Your Honour. 18824, I'm sorry. Sir, this was a document that you were shown the other day. Do you recognise the names on this list?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Yes. I can recognise all the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is written in the Cyrillic script. You understand the Cyrillic script?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Well, I'm finding it a bit harder to read handwritten letters. I can read capitals much better. But yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: May the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Are you able to recall the names of those five or six people?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Sefer Dzaferagic, Hamid Abdic, Mujo Cajic, Semso Omanovic, and perhaps two other people whose names escape me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what happened to these people on that day, that are named on this list?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: They were killed in 1992 and their bodies were discovered in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I suggest going into private session just briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland? We will admit the list of the names.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3361, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could go briefly back into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir at transcript page 4972 to 4973 you testified that when the first ten men were called out of the classroom and immediately after each of the men -- and immediately after each of the men were taken out, you heard bursts of fire. Are you able to recall the names of these ten men?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Yes. I know these names. Do I need to say them?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you are able to recall them.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Omer Dervisevic, Smail Abdic. Smail Abdic. Ale Cajic. Domazet, I did mention Smail. And then two brothers, Cehic, another Domazet. And well, I can't recall all the names at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified at transcript page 4973 that after these ten men were called out, the policemen who was guarding the classroom said, "Don't be afraid, it's the Green Berets who are attacking. We will calm them down and drive them away now. We will deal with that very quickly. There are quite a few of us here." What did you make of this remark?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, we did not even think that there were any Muslim Green Berets because not a single bullet was fired from our side in Biljani. Besides, most of the people were brought into the school building. We didn't even know why there was so much shooting initially, and we -- it only dawned on us later on that they were singling out these individuals, taking them and killing them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The ten men that you mentioned, have you ever seen them again?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: I've never seen them again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At transcript page 4975 you testified that when the bus was full, it started to move off and then it stopped, and at a point then four men were taken off the bus. Are you able to -- are you able to recall the names of the four men who were taken off the bus?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: I only recall two of them, namely Emir Abdic and -- I am having difficulty now recalling his name though I know the name -- the man, and I can see his face in my mind. No, I can't remember. I know his first name was Mujo. I can't remember the last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At transcript page 4976, you testified that you were taken off the bus with four other men and taken a few metres away to a house, and that you were subsequently shot at and you fell to the ground. You testified at transcript page 4978 that after you were lying still near the house after about ten minutes you heard the soldiers come to the front of the cafe and you said in your testimony that you could hear their conversations. What, if anything, did you hear them say?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Well, I was able to hear quite a bit. At one point as soldiers were going past the house one of them called to his colleagues and said, "Look here, there is quite a lot of the dead here as well." And I recall clearly one of them saying, "Well, I've had enough for today. I can't bear the sight of them any more." So they returned to the house which was also where the cafe was housed, and we could hear them rummaging around the cafe looking for a drink. One of them shouted, "Oh, I'd like to set all this on fire." To which the other responded, "No, it's a shame. It's too good a house." And so they spent around 20 minutes in conversation there, and then set out to leave the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified at transcript page 4984 that after the soldiers had left, you then hid in the area near your village until around the 10th -- the middle of September when you moved to the town of Kljuc. While you were hiding, what if anything did you observe in relation to the destruction of property, both civilian property and sacred sites?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Well, on the date of the event itself, the 10th of July, as I fled the place, I hid in the corn fields nearby. Quite often I would hear from the corn fields houses being set on fire, and there were already a few of them on fire. I think that quite a few houses burnt down that day. As I was moving about the village, I always tried to stay outside the perimeter of the village in order to be in control. I saw that on quite a few occasions houses were set on fire. In June or late June, a mosque was mined. Well, there was an attempt to blow it up, which was unsuccessful. And then five or six evenings later, I heard a very strong explosion. It was during the night. And in the morning, I looked toward the place where the mosque once stood, and the minaret was no longer to be seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said that was in June 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Yes, in June of 1992. Oh, I'm sorry, I beg your pardon. It was in June that all these events took place of cleansing up until the 10th of July. No it was in August. I'm sorry, it could not have been in June. I was hiding in the second half of July, and in early August. That's when these things could have happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could ask you now to look at the last document, and that is 65 ter number 11 -- sorry, 18825, sir, this was a document that you perused the other day. Do you recognise the names on this list?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is a list of 125 persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, the names on this list, do you know what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: They were all killed in 1992 except for five or six persons who survived, and I've said so already. So the list before and this list, together these six people survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, what physical or psychological effects, if any, do you suffer as a consequence of what you witnessed and endured in 1992 in the Kljuc municipality? And if you'd like to go into private session, please advise the Court.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I --?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, I have no further questions of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I may start my cross-examination and put the question I wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As a way of information, sir, if you feel you have to give some information that may reveal your identity, please don't hesitate to ask us to go into private session. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, are there any associated exhibits that are being tendered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for the reminder.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I seek to tender the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As well as the last one?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: First we will admit that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 18825 will be Exhibit P3362.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: With respect to one we would have an objection for 65 ter number 00897. Did you already have that flagged? That's an exhumation report and we didn't think that it was really an indispensable part of the testimony since only a few names were mentioned and we don't think it's a very sound basis to admit an entire exhumation report simply because the witness recognised a few names, all of which were contained in the transcript. So by reading the transcript you have all of the information you need from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You won't have problem if those pages containing those ten names referred to by the witness be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, not -- no, we wouldn't have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, do you have any observation? Actually, the witness was shown just one page. We are talking about the exhumation report but given the position of the -- whether -- given the position of the Defence and that the -- also in light of the definition of associated exhibits as being indispensable and inseparable part, separate from the other parts can be admitted as through bar table motion, I don't think they form indispensable and inseparable part but that's -- I'm speaking for myself and from the top of my head. Do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the pages that -- or the page that was shown to the witness, can be admitted. We can bar table the exhumation report. I think the exhumation report is an important document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there a real issue, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was thinking at some point we were going to have a witness who would testify to the exhumations and then we would have a chance to actually have Dr. Karadzic raise whatever issues he might choose to raise. I don't know that we have any dispute factually with respect to these victims or this site but it seems difficult to agree to admit an entire exhumation report simply on what material was presented in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, shall we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, among your last answers was the number of casualties from your village. So this is what I'd like to ask you. I don't want to mention the name of the village. Is it correct that in your village there were about 2.000 Muslims and about 400 to 500 Serbs, 25 per cent were Serbs, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it was for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm saying this to both you and myself. We have to pause between the questions and answers and the other way around. So it works both ways. So did you say, then, that 260 persons were killed, not 2006 persons as the transcript says?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Probably there was some confusion. 260 would be the right number, as far as casualties are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So could the transcript please be corrected? Tell us, then, how did these other persons get killed apart from the incident that you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: In Biljani, apart from 10 July, about 50 persons got killed on a few occasions, so all the others, around 200 of them were killed around 10 July except about 60 or 70 people were taken away to Kljuc. Now, since they would not have them either at Manjaca or elsewhere, they took them to Laniste and killed them. Now that I've started talking about this, the first man in Biljani was killed in the beginning of July. That's when the first cleansing took place, from the hamlet of Cehici, Hamdo Cehic was the man who was killed. After that, after this first killing took place, these 30 men who ended up in Manjaca were taken away on that day. Then, again, in mid-June, there was this other cleansing in Biljani where about 10 or 15 persons were killed in Biljani, among others Dzaferagic, Abid, and Tehvid Omanovic, and about 10 or 15 other persons, I'm not sure. About ten of them were killed in mid-June. Actually, after the 10th, about five or six or ten old men remained in the hamlet of Botunici after 10 July. So let's say until 20 July, that's when this happened, these ten old men were taken to a shed, practically they were killed there and torched. So that was from the end of June until the end of July that these killings took place in Biljani.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Out of all of this that you've told us about, what did you personally see?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: I personally saw the killing of five persons from the school, below a house. And then I saw also four men killed in front of me in Biljani. Then I personally saw the killing of my five friends, my four friends who were taken out with me on that day. As for the rest, I didn't see any of it except that I was in the corn fields that night and I heard trucks coming and bulldozers and collecting -- and they were collecting people. As I was lying below that house, I heard the soldier say, well, I have had enough of looking at the dead today. So this collecting of bodies went on late into the night, on seven or eight or ten times I heard them say, "There is some here as well, come here." There was only a couple of hundred metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A couple of hundred metres away from you, you heard a car and you heard their conversation, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the machine would not be heard then. Then it would be heard again. And that's the way it went until late that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statements, you said that in June 1991, some armed troops were freely moving about in that area that you're from. Tell me, what are these troops that could freely walk around armed and in uniform in June 1991?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: I don't know whether I said in June 1992. Perhaps the transcript has it wrong. It is June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: (redacted) And when columns of hundreds and hundreds of vehicles of the then-JNA, the Yugoslav army, were passing by that cafe, moving from Croatia towards Kljuc and further on, except that part of these troops stayed at Laniste. I was present when they came, I mean 25 men, volunteers, they themselves said that they were volunteers, they were given weapons. I personally made targets for them. They called me and I refused and I said that I wouldn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the sake of clarity, for the sake of the transcript, so that the participants, primarily the Trial Chamber, understand, you said in your statement of 3 June 2000, 1D4254 is the number I have, page 636, paragraph 5, you said this: Groups of armed Serbs often came to the cafe and, generally, you speak about this movement of the Serbs. Were these Serbs or was this the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: It was only Serbs that came to the cafe wearing JNA uniforms. The convoys of vehicles I saw were moving towards Laniste. I was standing by the road, only 20 or 30 metres away from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it is not some kind of Serb army but it is ethnic Serbs who were in the JNA, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on, do you know that in this ambush that we are going to discuss later, among the killed soldiers of the JNA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I seek a redaction on page 98, lines 23 and 24. And the -- up to the -- those two sentences, the first two sentences of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, agreed. Thank you. Let us continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, or did you know that in this ambush that your neighbours, Muslims from your municipality organised for the Yugoslav People's Army on the 25th and 27th of May, there were two Albanians among the killed soldiers and they were hanged after they were killed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about that. I did not hear that they were hanged. I heard that they were wounded during the ambush but I didn't realise that they were dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. So when we are talking about Serbs in 1991, we are talking about the JNA, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: The incident that you're talking about occurred in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But in other places, you also said that in 1991 the JNA used helicopters, landed and armed the Serbs. Do you know that already in 1991, Muslims and Croats, as you've confirmed yourself, did not want to respond to call-up for doing their compulsory military service, or being called up for the reserve because the war in Croatia was already under way?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: That was probably the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In some of your statements, you confirmed that you had been called up previously for exercises, for reservists, that you responded to that, that you received the usual compensation for that, but you said that you didn't want to do it in 1991, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: It is true that I responded beforehand but in 1991, I wasn't even called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So do you know that the JNA in 1991 had difficulties in manning its troops and there was a war going on in Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Well, I heard about that but to tell the truth I'm not really interested in that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I have to be interested because you mentioned the landing of helicopters and the arming of Serbs by the JNA. Do you know that these Serbs were reservists of the JNA, just as you were when you responded and also that they were under the command and control of the JNA regardless of whether they were there as reservists or whether from that reserve force they went to Croatia and came back? Do you know that these were JNA units?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: I find all of that clear but what is not clear to me is that each and every house could belong to the JNA. So in fact, weapons were being distribute from one house to the other. It's not that everybody was part of the JNA reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that for many municipalities, military records were hidden and that the JNA did not have full records so they had to go from house to house to see who wishes to respond to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: I have no information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement of 2000, that is 1D24, paragraph 6, you said that in that year, 1991, this was Serb propaganda and that you had opted for the Croats.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what you say: That there were major differences between Banja Luka and Sarajevo TV shows. Tell us, what were the differences?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, at that time there was thousands of different kinds of information bandied about. When you hear Banja Luka, you hear contradictory things about these situations. Inconceivable. Then in Sarajevo, they would say something completely different. So if you look at it that way, I preferred listening to the Croatian programme because I thought their reporting was more objective than both, because I sort of thought that they were in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But Banja Luka and Sarajevo are in the same republic, and Sarajevo TV programmes were in favour of Croats, and Banja Luka broadcasts were in favour of the Serbs in Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Quite honestly I don't know anything about any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also you said that when the war in Croatia started, the Muslims and Serbs were ordered to be mobilised, and the Muslims in our village, you say, refused to take military uniforms and go to Croatia, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the -- that responding to mobilisation is compulsory, according to the law, and that if one refuses to respond to the call-up, you have to be held accountable in any country in the world?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, if you're a pacifist you're not a military conscript but if you're a military conscript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer to the previous question? The interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what I said. I do apologise. Could you please say that once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question reads like this: [As read] "Do you agree that responding to mobilisation is compulsory according to the law, and that if one refuses to respond to the call-up you have to be held accountable in any country in the world."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said that I understood that and I said that I know that that is the responsibility of each and every citizen but if you go out to kill someone, then you can refuse. That's what I meant. I don't want to go to war and that is not what I wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, you did not receive a decision as a conscience objector. You did not get out of the army in a legal way, did you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know of anybody in your village or in your municipality who went to Croatia to help Croats to secede from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that there were Muslims who fought in Croatia while they were performing their regular military service, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did Croats from your village and from your municipality refuse to join the JNA and still they went to Croatia to volunteer and fight on the Croats' side?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you also mentioned that during the war in Croatia, Muslim men who refused to respond to the call-up had their movement abilities restricted. Why do you say that in 1991, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a country with regular authorities, Muslims had restricted movement if they had failed to respond to the call-ups and who was the one who restricted their movements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: I don't know who it was. I'm not really the right person to answer that but I know when the war started in Croatia, they couldn't leave because the check-points had already been erected on the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina and those were manned by the former JNA, the former army members, and they could not go to Croatia. I really don't know much about that. This is too complicated for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. What you have just told us, then, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Yes, apparently so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D4258, page 6 in e-court, is the document in question. And what you have just told us is that restrictions were introduced after the war broke out in Croatia, and when you say that you meant the restrictions on leaving Bosnia and entering Croatia, right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-075
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
